newsitem.title: USA: US exchanges say "pro-exemption" talks to continue.
newsitem.headline: US exchanges say "pro-exemption" talks to continue.

text.p: Chicago's futures exchanges testified to Congress this week in favor of a revamped Commodity Exchange Act, but said they would continue to seek a compromise with U.S. regulators on the bill's central provision, "pro-market exemption."
"Pro-market is the key ingredient toward addressing the competitive fairness issue in the bill," Mark Young, the Chicago Board of Trade's outside counsel, said in an interview.
Pro-market exemption, a provision in both the House and Senate versions of a bill to amend the CEA, would exclude certain transactions by professional traders from federal regulation.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission and Securities and Exchange Commission are both opposed to pro-market exemption.

U.S. futures exchange officials testified in House hearings, which finished on Thursday, that U.S. futures exchanges had seen their share of the global market decline in recent years because of U.S. regulation of their markets. They say regulation is less burdensome in over-the-counter and overseas markets.

"Business is done where the real costs, including costs to sophisticated traders imposed by regulations that are designed to protect small investors, are least burdensome," Chicago Mercantile Exchange chairman Jack Sandner told the House Agriculture subcommittee.

In the meantime, officials at both exchanges said they had been meeting weekly with Commodity Futures Trading Commission officials in an effort to reach a compromise on various provisions of the bill, including cost-benefit analysis and the contract approval process as well as pro-market exemption.
"I think the pro-market (exemption) will be the one area where they (the exchanges and CFTC) probably disagree the most," Rep. Thomas Ewing, an Illinois Republican, said in an interview.
Ewing, who heads the subcommittee that held this week's hearings, said most provisions in the bill he introduced last fall will be modified at the committee level.
He said he expected to see "improvements" in the original pro-market exemption provision.
"It will probably move in the direction of deregulation without raising unwarranted fears among those who are strong advocates of regulation," Ewing said.

Neither the CBOT nor the CME have implemented Par 36, a three-year pilot program the CFTC granted all U.S. exchanges in 1995. The program would permit some transactions to trade with some regulatory relief from the CFTC.
Exchange officials said the pilot program was too costly to implement and did not provide enough regulatory relief.
"The relief is not sufficient to warrant the capital, research and development expenditure of putting a product in pro-market," the CBOT's Young said.

A CME spokeswoman said the exchange was not looking to immediately designate one of its contracts as pro-market, but rather wanted the option to designate a market quickly without regulatory approval from the CFTC.
William Brodsky, president of the Chicago Board Options Exchange, testified against the House bill on behalf of nine securities self-regulatory organizations.

A CBOE spokesman said Brodsky, who had previously testified in favor of the bill as president of the CME, spoke against pro-exemption only in regard to equity-based derivatives. ((Derivatives desk 312-408-8750))
